stem: Explain why the Lancaster House Conference succeeded.

points.description: The war: Rhodesia could not win; martial law, emigration, failing economy.
Frontline States (Mozambique, Zambia) pressed the Patriotic Front to settle.
Britain took direct responsibility for the transition.
Commonwealth/international pressure: Zimbabwe-Rhodesia not recognised.
Compromises, e.g. land clauses accepted after informal funding assurances.
A monitored ceasefire and elections gave both sides confidence.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: By 1979 the Rhodesian forces could not win: martial law covered most of the country, whites were leaving and the economy was failing. Mozambique and Zambia, suffering raids, pressed the Patriotic Front to accept a deal. Britain took direct charge of the transition through a Governor, solving the problem that had broken up Geneva. The Commonwealth and other states refused to recognise Zimbabwe-Rhodesia. The Patriotic Front accepted the land clauses after informal assurances of funding, and a Commonwealth-monitored ceasefire with elections gave both sides confidence.

hints: Think about pressures on each side and what was new at Lancaster House.

stem: Explain **two** reasons why the Victoria Falls conference of 1975 failed.

points.description: Identifies Smith's refusal to accept majority rule.
Explains: without this there was nothing the nationalists could accept.
Identifies disputes over conditions for further talks / divisions among nationalist leaders.
Explains: e.g. no agreement on immunity for exiled leaders, so talks could not continue inside Rhodesia.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Smith still would not accept majority rule, so there was no basis for agreement. The two sides also argued about conditions for further talks inside Rhodesia, such as immunity from arrest for exiled leaders, and the nationalist leaders, though nominally united under Muzorewa, were divided among themselves.

hints: Think about Smith's position and the nationalists' position.

stem:
Study the sources and answer the questions.

**Source A** — a broadcast by a fictional Zimbabwe-Rhodesia government spokesman, April 1979 (invented for this question)

> For the first time in our history every adult has voted, and an African Prime Minister will lead the nation. The terrorists who refused to take part have shown that they want power by the gun, not by the ballot. The world must now recognise our new government.

**Source B** — an editorial in a fictional newspaper in Lusaka, Zambia, May 1979 (invented for this question)

> An African face in the Prime Minister's office changes nothing while the generals, the judges and the police chiefs remain the same, and while a quarter of parliament can block any change. The men fighting in the bush were not invited. This is not majority rule; it is minority rule in disguise.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: What does Source A claim had been achieved in April 1979?

points.description: Every adult had voted for the first time.
An African Prime Minister would lead the country.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: How does Source B challenge the claims of Source A? Use details from both sources.

points.description: A says majority rule had come; B says it is minority rule in disguise.
B: security forces and judges unchanged (whites kept control).
B: a quarter of parliament can block change (28 white seats).
B: the fighters were excluded; A calls them terrorists who refused to take part.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Which source gives the more accurate view of the Internal Settlement? Use both sources and your own knowledge.

points.description: A: government propaganda seeking recognition; one-sided.
A accurate that all adults voted and Muzorewa became PM.
B: from Zambia, a Frontline State hostile to the settlement; one-sided too.
B supported by own knowledge: 28 of 100 white seats, white control of army, police, judiciary.
Own knowledge: no recognition, war intensified, Patriotic Front excluded.
Supported judgement.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Source A was broadcast by the Zimbabwe-Rhodesia government to win recognition, so it stresses the achievements: all adults voted in April 1979 and Muzorewa became Prime Minister, which is true. Source B comes from a newspaper in Zambia, a Frontline State that supported the Patriotic Front, so it is also one-sided. But its claims are supported by own knowledge: whites held 28 of the 100 seats, enough to block constitutional change, and they kept control of the army, police, judiciary and civil service. The Patriotic Front was excluded, the war intensified and no country recognised the government. Source B gives the more accurate view of where real power lay, although Source A is right that the election was a change in form.

parts.explanation: Weigh both sources against own knowledge.

hints: Compare the claims of each source with the facts of the 1979 constitution.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
In important ways Lancaster House was a victory for the Patriotic Front. It brought elections on the basis of one person, one vote, which ZANU and ZAPU had demanded since 1957, and it set aside Muzorewa's government and the Internal Settlement, from which the Patriotic Front had been excluded.

However, the Patriotic Front also made major concessions. Twenty seats were reserved for whites for seven years. The Bill of Rights protected property, and for ten years land could be bought only from willing sellers, which slowed the redistribution of land that had been a central aim of the struggle. The Patriotic Front accepted these terms partly because Mozambique and Zambia pressed it to settle.

Overall it was a victory on the main issue, majority rule, but a compromise on land, which left problems for independent Zimbabwe.

parts.explanation: Top level weighs gains and concessions.

hints: In (b), consider what each side gained and gave up.
